marrow__PHYSIO_CH22_Q011.takeaway: The normal adult P50 is approximately 27 mmHg.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH22_Q011.displayText: P50 is the PO₂ at which Hb is 50% saturated and indexes Hb–O₂ affinity. Normal adult Hb has a P50 of about 27 mmHg. A higher P50 means lower oxygen affinity and a right-shifted dissociation curve; a lower P50 means higher affinity and a left shift.

rationales.b: 45 mmHg is not the adult Hb P50; 27 mmHg corresponds to 50% saturation.
rationales.c: 10 mmHg would indicate a much higher affinity than normal adult hemoglobin.
rationales.d: 100 mmHg is near alveolar PO₂, not the PO₂ for 50% Hb saturation.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH22_Q012.takeaway: Lower pH reduces Hb affinity and shifts the oxygen curve right, promoting O₂ unloading.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH22_Q012.displayText: A decrease in pH shifts the oxygen–hemoglobin dissociation curve to the right (Bohr effect), lowering Hb affinity and helping unload O₂ to metabolically active tissue. Increased CO₂, temperature, and 2,3-DPG also shift right; hypoxia, hypercarbia, reduced pH, exercise, and increased anaerobic glycolysis are associated conditions. Growth hormone, thyroid hormone, and androgen can increase 2,3-DPG. A left shift reflects higher affinity, as with alkalosis, reduced CO₂, lower 2,3-DPG, or hypothermia.

rationales.b: A left shift increases Hb affinity and favors loading, the opposite of the effect of lower pH.
rationales.c: Lower pH does shift the dissociation curve; it does not leave it unchanged.
rationales.d: The source’s direction is a right shift when pH falls.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH22_Q013.takeaway: Each myoglobin binds one O₂, so four myoglobin molecules bind four O₂ molecules.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH22_Q013.displayText: Four molecules of myoglobin bind four O₂ molecules because each myoglobin molecule has one heme and binds one oxygen molecule. Myoglobin’s O₂-dissociation curve is a rectangular hyperbola and lies to the left of the sigmoid hemoglobin curve, reflecting its higher affinity and role as an O₂ store in muscle.

rationales.b: Each myoglobin binds one O₂, not four; four myoglobin molecules bind four O₂.
rationales.c: One O₂ is bound per myoglobin molecule, so four molecules bind more than one O₂ total.
rationales.d: Sixteen would require each myoglobin molecule to bind four O₂ molecules.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH22_Q014.takeaway: The Bohr effect’s pH/CO₂-mediated right shift promotes tissue O₂ unloading.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH22_Q014.displayText: The Bohr effect facilitates O₂ delivery to tissues. Increased tissue metabolism produces CO₂, which enters blood, raises carbonic acid and H⁺, lowers pH, and reduces Hb affinity for oxygen; the O₂–Hb dissociation curve shifts right and unloads O₂. In the lungs, CO₂ leaves blood, H⁺ falls, the curve shifts left, and Hb affinity rises for O₂ loading. In the placenta, fetal blood arrives with more CO₂; CO₂ diffuses into maternal blood. Fetal CO₂ and H⁺ then fall, shifting fetal Hb left and promoting O₂ loading, while maternal CO₂ and H⁺ rise, shifting maternal Hb right and promoting O₂ release. This double Bohr effect assists transfer.

rationales.b: The effect described is primarily pH/CO₂ regulation of Hb oxygen affinity and unloading, not CO₂ transport itself.
rationales.c: Chloride transport through the RBC anion exchanger is the chloride shift, not the Bohr effect.
rationales.d: Bohr effect facilitates tissue oxygen unloading and therefore O₂ transport; “none” is incorrect.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH22_Q015.takeaway: Acidosis inhibits red-cell glycolysis and decreases 2,3-DPG.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH22_Q015.displayText: The level of 2,3-DPG is decreased in acidosis. Acidosis inhibits red-cell glycolysis, which reduces 2,3-DPG generated from the glycolytic intermediate 3-phosphoglycerate. Since 2,3-DPG binds deoxyhemoglobin and reduces O₂ affinity, the lower concentration in acidosis shifts Hb toward greater oxygen affinity relative to high-DPG conditions. Anemia, high altitude, and exercise typically increase 2,3-DPG as an adaptation to improve tissue O₂ release.
emphasis: The level of 2,3-DPG is decreased in acidosis.

rationales.a: Anemia generally raises 2,3-DPG over time to promote oxygen unloading.
rationales.c: High altitude increases 2,3-DPG as an adaptive response to hypoxia.
rationales.d: Exercise and increased tissue demand tend to increase 2,3-DPG, not decrease it.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH22_Q016.takeaway: HbF binds 2,3-DPG weakly through its γ chains, increasing O₂ affinity.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH22_Q016.displayText: Increased affinity of HbF to O2 is due to weak 2,3-DPG binding by its γ chains compared with the β chains of adult HbA. Adult β chains are replaced by γ chains in fetal hemoglobin; with less 2,3-DPG bound, HbF has a left-shifted O₂ dissociation curve and lower P50. This higher affinity supports O₂ transfer from maternal blood to the fetus despite fetal PaO₂ of only about 40 mmHg.
emphasis: Increased affinity of HbF to O2

rationales.b: HbF has decreased, not increased, binding to 2,3-DPG; this underlies its higher O₂ affinity.
rationales.c: A rise in pH is not the structural reason HbF has higher oxygen affinity.
rationales.d: Lower hemoglobin concentration does not explain HbF’s left shift; γ-chain interaction with DPG does.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH22_Q017.takeaway: Oxygen binding to Hb in the lungs promotes CO₂ release: the Haldane effect.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH22_Q017.displayText: Binding of O2 with hemoglobin tends to displace CO2 from the blood. This Haldane effect occurs when oxygenation in the lungs makes Hb a stronger acid and promotes CO₂ release into alveoli. Conversely, deoxygenated Hb in tissues carries more CO₂ and buffers H⁺. This facilitates CO₂ transport and contributes to the leftward shift of the O₂–Hb curve in lungs.
emphasis: Binding of O2 with hemoglobin tends to displace CO2 from the blood.

rationales.b: This reverses the Haldane effect; it is oxygenation of Hb that promotes CO₂ release.
rationales.c: HCO₃⁻ leaving RBC in exchange for chloride is the chloride shift.
rationales.d: The described O₂-dependent release of CO₂ is the Haldane effect, so this is not “none.”

marrow__PHYSIO_CH22_Q018.takeaway: Chloride shift adds osmotically active ions to venous RBCs, drawing in water and raising PCV.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH22_Q018.displayText: PCV is higher in venous blood: venous hematocrit/packed cell volume is about 3% higher than arterial PCV for two source-described reasons. First, the chloride shift accompanies tissue CO₂ entry: carbonic anhydrase forms H₂CO₃, which dissociates to H⁺ and HCO₃⁻; H⁺ is buffered by deoxyhemoglobin, and HCO₃⁻ exits RBCs through AE1/Band 3 in exchange for Cl⁻. The extra osmotically active anion (HCO₃⁻ or Cl⁻) draws water into RBCs, increasing their volume; venous RBC chloride content is higher. Second, a small amount of arterial fluid returns through lymphatics rather than veins, further concentrating venous blood.

rationales.a: The Haldane effect concerns O₂-dependent CO₂ carriage; it is not the cellular-volume mechanism asked here.
rationales.b: The Bohr effect shifts Hb affinity with pH/CO₂; the PCV difference is explained by chloride shift and fluid return.
rationales.d: 2,3-DPG affects Hb–O₂ affinity, not the venous–arterial PCV difference.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH22_Q019.takeaway: CPDA’s phosphate-containing solution limits the storage-related fall in 2,3-DPG.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH22_Q019.displayText: The fall in 2, 3 DPG is less when the blood is stored in CPDA compared with ACD. CPDA (citrate, phosphate, dextrose, adenine) preserves 2,3-DPG better than ACD (acid citrate dextrose). Because 2,3-DPG binds deoxyhemoglobin, higher retained DPG lowers Hb oxygen affinity, raises P50, shifts the curve right, and improves O₂ release to tissues after transfusion. Stored blood still loses DPG over time, but less in phosphate-containing CPDA.
emphasis: The fall in 2, 3 DPG is less

rationales.b: Retained 2,3-DPG reduces Hb affinity and increases oxygen release; CPDA does not cause decreased release.
rationales.c: More retained DPG raises P50 rather than lowering it.
rationales.d: CPDA’s advantage is phosphate-mediated DPG preservation, not simply being less acidic.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH22_Q020.takeaway: Use the in-vivo Hüfner constant: 1.31 mL O₂/g × 14 g/dL ≈ 18.3 mL/dL.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH22_Q020.displayText: The oxygen carrying capacity of a boy with haemoglobin 14 g/dL is estimated with Hüfner’s constant: each gram of hemoglobin carries about 1.31 mL O₂ because normal blood includes inactive Hb derivatives. For Hb 14 g/dL, capacity = 1.31 × 14 = 18.34 mL O₂/dL, approximately 18. The theoretical amount for fully saturated normal Hb is about 1.39 mL/g, but the in-vivo value is lower. The O₂–Hb curve relates PO₂ to saturation; systemic arterial blood usually has PO₂ around 95 mmHg and saturation near 97%, while venous blood at PO₂ around 40 mmHg is about 75% saturated.

rationales.a: 22 mL/dL would require a larger capacity per gram than the in-vivo value of 1.31 mL/g.
rationales.c: 14 mL/dL incorrectly treats each gram of Hb as carrying only 1 mL O₂.
